item.title: sshcert-authorize
item.description:
sshd asks it, for each certificate login, which principals may log into the account. It answers with the account’s principals only if the certificate’s domain grant names this host; otherwise it answers nothing, and sshd refuses the certificate. It takes the arguments, flags, output and log format of GÉANT’sssh-cert-authorize, and differs in what it refuses.

How sshd calls it 

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/efp-ssh-ca.pub
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand /usr/local/bin/sshcert-authorize %u %k
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommandUser nobody
install -o root -g root -m 0755 sshcert-authorize /usr/local/bin/
echo login.example.org > /etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf

and, for each local account, the principals that may log into it, one per line,in /etc/ssh/auth_principals/<account>. sshd runs the command only from a path owned by root and writable by nobody else.

%u is the account being logged into. %k is the certificate, base64; a wholessh-...-cert-v01@openssh.com BASE64 line is read too, and when the argument is absent the certificate is read from standard input. A third argument, when one is given (sshd’s %t), must be the certificate’s type, or the certificate is refused.

exit prints sshd
0 the account’s principals, one per line lets the certificate in if one of its principals is among them
1 nothing refuses it
2 nothing refuses it: the arguments were wrong

It does not check the signature, the CA or the validity dates

Nothing in the command verifies the certificate’s signature or its validity window: sshd, which trusts the CA through TrustedUserCAKeys,does that. The command decides one question, whether the certificate is meant for this host and this account.

What it refuses

In the order it checks:

  1. an account name that is empty, ., .., or holds /, \ or a NUL;
  2. a host with no domain configured, or one that is not a valid host name;
  3. a certificate that does not parse, a plain key, or a host certificate;
  4. a %t that is not the certificate’s type;
  5. with --krl, a certificate the list revokes, or every certificate when the list cannot be read or has expired;
  6. a domain grant that is present and malformed, whatever the flags;
  7. no domain grant at all, unless --allow-no-grant;
  8. a grant none of whose patterns matches any of the host’s names;
  9. an account with no principals file, or an empty one.

The host’s names are --domain, or the variable --domain-env names, or the lines of --domain-file (blank lines and # comments ignored; several lines are several names, any of which may match).

Against certificates signed by a test CA for the account alice, whose principals file lists a1b2c3@univ-example.example, on a host calledlogin.hpc.example.org:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
a1b2c3@univ-example.example

The last line is the answer sshd reads; the lines before it are the log, here on standard error. A certificate granted other hosts:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-other-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1003 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example other host" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="domain not granted" grant=["*.elsewhere.example.net"] serial=1003 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q

A certificate with no grant:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no domain grant" serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q

An account with no principals file, and a plain key:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals bob "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=denied user=bob domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no principals file for the user" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice.pub)"
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="a ssh-ed25519 key, not a certificate"

Each of these exited 1, and printed nothing on standard output.

Why a certificate with no grant is refused

GÉANT’s ssh-cert-authorize lets a certificate with no domain grant through(“might be valid for non-domain-based auth”), and one whose grant it cannot parse, or that is empty. Then a site that trusts two CAs inTrustedUserCAKeys (the federation’s, and its own for staff, or a test CA)lets a certificate from the second CA in on every host, for any principal in a principals file, with no domain check at all. The domain filter is only a filter if a certificate that does not say where it may be used is refused.

A site that really wants GÉANT’s behaviour says so, and the command logs each time it applies it:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --allow-no-grant --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=no_grant_allowed user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
a1b2c3@univ-example.example

Even then, a grant that is present but malformed is refused.

--krl

RevokedKeys is sshd’s own check, made before the command runs, for every key and certificate, and it also revokes a CA key; prefer it. --krl FILE checks an OpenSSH KRL inside the command, and adds what sshd does not do: it refusesevery certificate once the list has expired (its expires@go-authn.github.io extension, which sshd ignores), and every certificate when the list cannot be read. A list with no expiry is used without one.

Three runs: with the KRL authn-revokd writes, first a current one, then the fail-closed one it writes when the issuer’s list lapses; and last with--krl naming a file that does not exist:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
a1b2c3@univ-example.example
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="certificate revoked" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl missing.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="KRL unreadable: open missing.krl: no such file or directory" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q

The second run is refused because the fail-closed list revokes the certificate’s CA key: the check covers the certificate’s own key, its serial and key ID, and the key that signed it. The third is refused because the list cannot be read: no list is not taken to mean nothing revoked.

Flags 

$ sshcert-authorize -help
usage: sshcert-authorize [flags] USER [CERTIFICATE [KEYTYPE]]
An sshd AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand (%u %k) that refuses a certificate whose
ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension does not grant this host, or that has none.
-allow-no-grant
let in a certificate with no domain grant (GÉANT's behaviour); a malformed grant is still refused
-debug
log details
-domain string
the host's domain (overrides --domain-env and --domain-file)
-domain-env string
environment variable holding the host's domain
-domain-file string
file holding the host's domain, one name per line (default "/etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf")
-extension string
name of the domain-grant extension (default "ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org")
-krl string
refuse certificates this OpenSSH KRL revokes, and every certificate once it has expired or cannot be read
-principals-dir string
directory of principals files, one per user (default "/etc/ssh/auth_principals")
-syslog
log to syslog, facility AUTH (--syslog=false: to stderr) (default true)
-version
print the version and exit

Logs are key=value lines (action=cert_processed, action=denied,action=authorized, with serial and ca_fingerprint), to syslog, facility AUTH, by default. sshd discards the command’s standard error, so keep syslog on in production; --debug also writes everything to standard error. A value that comes from the client, such as the account name, is quoted when it holds a space, =, a quote or a control character, so it cannot forge a log field.

-version prints the module version, in a release binary and in one built by go install alike:

$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.7
$ sshcert-authorize -version
sshcert-authorize v0.1.7

Before v0.1.5, a binary from go install printed sshcert-authorize dev.

item.title: sshcert
item.description:
A certificate from a federation’s CA is not, by itself, permission for every host that trusts that CA. The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA writes the hosts a certificate is meant for into an extension,ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org, and sshd ignores it. go-authn/sshcert reads and writes that extension, and its command, sshcert-authorize, is whatsshd runs to enforce it. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0. These pages describe v0.1.7.

$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.7
$ sshcert-authorize -version
sshcert-authorize v0.1.7
sshcert-authorize the AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: what it checks, what it refuses, and how sshd calls it

The extension

Its data is a compact JSON array of host patterns, ["login.example.org"]. A* matches one or more characters within a single label, and names compare without case:

pattern matches does not match
login.example.org login.example.org, LOGIN.example.org www.login.example.org
*.example.org a.example.org example.org, a.b.example.org
prod-*.example.org prod-1.example.org prod-.example.org
*.*.example.org a.b.example.org a.example.org

The reading is strict: only what the encoder writes is accepted. No whitespace, nothing after ], no JSON escapes, no duplicates, at most 64 patterns, each made of letters, digits, hyphens and *, in labels of 1 to 63 bytes, at most 253 bytes, and no * in the rightmost label. null, objects,numbers and nested arrays are refused. [] is accepted, and grants no host.

A grant that is present and malformed is never reported as absent. That difference is the whole point of the command.

Who uses it

  • authn-bridge writes the extension for a client’s ssh_domain_grants, after checking each pattern with this package’s ValidatePattern.
  • go-fileshare’s SFTP server reads it with ssh_domains, and refuses a certificate with no grant unless ssh_accept_ungranted is set.
  • sshcert-authorize is the same check for a plain sshd.

Licence

BSD-3-Clause.

item.title: Certificates
item.description:
A person who logged in can have an SSH public key certified, or an X.509 client certificate issued, for a few hours. A server that trusts the provider’s CA lets them in with no account file to edit there. Every certificate is recorded incertificates_file before it is handed out: one that cannot be recorded is not issued, since it could never be revoked, and revoked ones are published in the KRL and the CRL.

SSH certificates 

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

ssh_ca {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/ssh-ca" # authn-bridge keygen --ssh-ca; Ed25519
 validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most
}

client "sftp" {
 device = true
 ssh_certificates = true
}

authn-bridge ssh-cert --issuer https://login.example.org --client sftp logs in with a code, posts ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (or --key) to/ssh/certificate with a token of the ssh scope, and writes<key>-cert.pub beside it, where ssh and sftp find it.

The CA key must be Ed25519: an RSA CA key signs with SHA-1 unless told otherwise, which OpenSSH has refused by default since 8.8.

What the certificate says.

  • Exactly one principal, the person’s preferred_username unless the client’s profile says another claim. A certificate with no principal is valid for any user (PROTOCOL.certkeys), so a person with no username gets none. A name holding a comma, a space, a quote, a backslash or a control character is refused (403): sshd reads principals="a,b" and AuthorizedPrincipalsFile entries as lists, so one such name is two.
  • Key ID <principal> sub=<sub> jti=<token id>: what sshd logs.
  • No permit-* extension by default. SFTP needs none, and a certificate that permits no pty, no forwarding and no rc file grants file access and nothing else.
  • The person’s groups in the groups@go-authn.org extension, one per line,when the token carries groups. OpenSSH ignores it; it is signed, so a server that authorizes by group can believe it.
  • Valid from five minutes ago (for clocks that disagree) until validity from now, or until the IdP’s session ends if that is sooner.
  • The key must be Ed25519, ECDSA P-256/384/521, a security key (sk-), or RSA of at least 2048 bits. A certificate is refused as a key.

The EuroHPC SSH CA profile

The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA (GÉANT / MyAccessID) issues Ed25519 certificates valid one hour, with one principal that names the person across the federation, and the hosts they are meant for in GÉANT’sssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension. A client can have its certificates issued in that shape. Every key is per client and optional; a client that sets none gets the certificate above.

client "efp" {
 device = true
 ssh_certificates = true
 ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id" # the default is preferred_username
 ssh_validity = "1h" # never longer than ssh_ca's, nor the IdP's session
 ssh_extensions = ["permit-pty"] # none by default
 ssh_domain_grants = ["login.hpc.example.org"] # the hosting entity's hosts
 # ssh_source_address = ["192.0.2.0/24"] # the source-address critical option
}
key
ssh_principal_claim preferred_username, sub, voperson_id or eduperson_principal_name. The last two are released by the eduperson scope, which the token must hold (authn-bridge ssh-cert --scope eduperson); otherwise, or when the IdP released no such attribute, the answer is 403 saying which
ssh_extensions among permit-pty, permit-user-rc, permit-port-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-X11-forwarding
ssh_source_address addresses or CIDR prefixes, written canonically into source-address
ssh_validity never longer than ssh_ca’s validity (equal is accepted), for this client
ssh_domain_grants domain patterns, checked by go-authn/sshcert’s ValidatePattern and encoded by its EncodeDomainGrant

What the profile refuses

Each at startup, from authn-bridge check:

authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_validity = 24h0m0s: longer than the ssh_ca validity, 12h0m0s
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_extensions: "no-touch-required" is not one of permit-X11-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-port-forwarding, permit-pty, permit-user-rc
authn-bridge: client "src": ssh_source_address: "192.0.2.1/24" has bits set under its mask: 192.0.2.0/24?
authn-bridge: client "x": ssh_principal_claim, ssh_extensions, ssh_source_address, ssh_validity and ssh_domain_grants shape SSH certificates: they need ssh_certificates = true

no-touch-required is not offered: it waives the user-presence test of the person’s own security key, which is not the provider’s to give away for everybody of a client.

A domain grant is held to the specification’s syntax, then to this provider’s own policy: lower case, at least two labels, and a wildcard only under a registrable domain. What stays fixed to the right of the last wildcard must not be a public suffix (the Public Suffix List): *.ac.uk would grant every institution under it.

authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "*.ac.uk": a wildcard over the public suffix "ac.uk" grants every domain under it
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "Login.hpc.example.org": written in lower case, as hosting entities' domains are compared
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "login.hpc.*": sshcert: invalid domain pattern: pattern "login.hpc.*" has a wildcard in its rightmost label

Trusting it from a site

GET /ssh/config publishes the CA key in the shape EFP publishes its own, so a site follows EFP’s trust instructions with this provider’s URL:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/config
{"PublicKey":"ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje"}
curl -s https://login.example.org/ssh/config | jq -r '.PublicKey' > /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub
echo "TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config

sshd ignores the domain grant. The site filters by it with anAuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: sshcert-authorize,which refuses a certificate whose grant does not name the host, and one with no grant at all. The CA is not in the OpenID discovery document: no OpenID Connect metadata names an SSH CA.

What remains different from EFP’s own CA: with ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id", as above, the principal is the subject-id the person’s institution released, in lower case, not a MyAccessID identifier; the groups extension is there when the token carries groups; and there is a KRL,GET /ssh/krl, listing the certificates of people disabled here.

X.509 client certificates, for NFS over TLS

NFS over TLS (RFC 9289) can name the client by its certificate.

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

x509_ca {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.key" # authn-bridge keygen --x509-ca /var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca
 cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.crt" # what go-fileshare trusts
 validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most
}

client "nfs" {
 device = true
 x509_certificates = true
}

authn-bridge nfs-cert --issuer ... --client nfs makes a P-256 key on the person’s machine, posts a certificate request to /x509/cert with a token of the nfs scope, and writes the certificate and the key. The CA key must be P-256, and its certificate a CA that signs certificates and CRLs.

What the certificate says. The request’s subject and extensions are ignored: what is certified is the token’s person, not what they asked for.

  • The person, user@domain, as one subjectAltName otherName 1.3.6.1.4.1.2238.1.1.1 holding a UTF8String, where FreeBSD’srpc.tlsservd -u reads it. A username without @, or under three bytes, is refused.
  • Each group as a URI name beside it:tag:go-authn.github.io,2026:group:<the group, percent-encoded>.
  • The CN is the username; past 64 characters the subject is empty and the subjectAltName critical (RFC 5280).
  • Client authentication only, and a CRL distribution point:<issuer>/x509/crl.
  • Valid from five minutes ago until validity, the IdP’s session or the CA’s own certificate, whichever ends first.
  • A P-256 or RSA (2048 bits and more) key, and a request signed by it.

A certificate names the machine, not the user of it

RFC 9289: the server “cannot utilize the remote TLS peer identity to authenticate RPC users”. Linux sets the client certificate per mount, so everybody using that mount is the person it names. This is for a machine one person uses, and authn-bridge nfs-cert says so.

A certificate request held open across a disabling

The token is checked when the request starts and the body read after, at whatever pace the client sends it. So a certificate is recorded first, and then the token and the person are checked again: if the person was disabled, or the token revoked, in between, the certificate just recorded is revoked and the answer is 401. Either the revocation saw the certificate, or the certificate sees the revocation.

item.title: krl — OpenSSH key revocation lists
item.description:
Is this SSH certificate or key revoked — as sshd would answer? The binary format of OpenSSH’s PROTOCOL.krl, the list sshd loads throughRevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -k writes. golang.org/x/crypto/ssh has no support for it.

go get github.com/go-authn/krl@v0.6.1

IsRevoked follows ssh_krl_check_key in OpenSSH’s krl.c: a certificate is revoked when its serial or key ID is revoked under the CA that signed it or under any CA, when its CA key is revoked, or when its own key is revoked by blob or by SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint. Serial 0 — what a CA writes when it names none — is never revoked by serial.

Example 

package main

import (
 "crypto/ed25519"
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/krl"
 "golang.org/x/crypto/ssh"
)

func main() {
 ca := signer()
 user := signer()

 // The issuer: certificate 42 is revoked, and so is everything for key ID "alice".
 b := krl.NewBuilder(7, "revoked by the bridge")
 b.RevokeSerial(ca.PublicKey(), 42)
 b.RevokeKeyID(nil, "alice") // nil: under any CA
 b.SetExpires(time.Now().Add(time.Hour))
 data, err := b.Marshal(time.Now())
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 // The server: parse the list, then ask about each certificate.
 k, err := krl.Parse(data)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fmt.Println("version", k.Version, "signed", k.Signed, "expires set", !k.Expires.IsZero())
 for _, c := range []struct {
 serial uint64
 id string
 }{{42, "bob"}, {43, "bob"}, {44, "alice"}} {
 fmt.Println(c.serial, c.id, k.IsRevoked(certificate(ca, user.PublicKey(), c.serial, c.id)))
 }
}

func signer() ssh.Signer {
 _, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
 s, _ := ssh.NewSignerFromKey(priv)
 return s
}

func certificate(ca ssh.Signer, key ssh.PublicKey, serial uint64, id string) *ssh.Certificate {
 c := &ssh.Certificate{
 Key: key, Serial: serial, KeyId: id, CertType: ssh.UserCert,
 ValidPrincipals: []string{id}, ValidBefore: ssh.CertTimeInfinity,
 }
 if err := c.SignCert(rand.Reader, ca); err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 return c
}
version 7 signed false expires set true
42 bob true
43 bob false
44 alice true

The same list and certificates, written to files, get the same three answers from OpenSSH 10.3p1’s ssh-keygen -Q -f list.krl: REVOKED, ok,REVOKED.

Expiry: expires@go-authn.github.io

A KRL has a generation date and a version, and nothing says when it stops being current, so a stale copy cannot be told from a fresh one.Builder.SetExpires writes that time in an extension section namedExtensionExpires, not critical, so sshd and ssh-keygen load the list and ignore it; Parse reads it into KRL.Expires.

No signatures

OpenSSH never exposed a way to write the KRL signature section and no longer verifies it. Parse skips one and sets Signed, which says nothing about authenticity; Builder never writes one. The list’s integrity, and so its expiry’s, comes from its transport — HTTPS from an authenticated server — or from a detached SSHSIG signature checked by the caller, which this package does not do.

Merging: one file for sshd

sshd read a single RevokedKeys file until OpenSSH 10.3, so a server trusting several CAs needs their lists in one. Builder.Merge adds every revocation of a parsed list. Builder.MergeCA(k, ca, others...) keeps k’s section for ca, its any-CA sections re-scoped to ca, and its explicit keys and fingerprints, and leaves out — counting them — sections for another CA and keys or fingerprints that designate one of others. MergeCAWith withMergeOptions{DropKeys: true} also leaves out every explicit key exceptca’s own, for a list not trusted with every CA’s users: a revoked user key locks that user out under every CA of the merged file, because sshd checks a certificate’s own key whoever signed it.

What it refuses, and why

Parse refuses what ssh-keygen and sshd refuse: a bad magic or format version, truncated or trailing data, an unknown section or certificate subsection, an unknown extension marked critical, a CA key OpenSSH cannot parse, serial 0, an inverted serial range, a bitmap larger than OpenSSH reads or one that wraps past 2^64−1. It also refuses a malformed or repeated expiry:read as absent, it would turn a list meant to lapse into one that never does.

Builder refuses — at Marshal, which returns the first invalid request —serial 0, a range whose low end is 0 or above its high end, a key ID or comment containing a NUL, a certificate given where a CA key is expected, and an expiry before the generation date.

One deliberate difference. For many sparse serials close together,ssh-keygen -k writes a bitmap wider than its own reader accepts and then refuses its own file (bignum is too large). Parse refuses that file too,as sshd would; Builder starts a new section before a bitmap gets that wide, so what it writes is always readable.

Parse allocates in proportion to what the list revokes, as OpenSSH does: a KRL should come from a source trusted not to send an enormous one.

What it is checked against

OpenSSH’s ssh-keygen, on the Linux and macOS lanes, whereKRL_REQUIRE_SSHKEYGEN=1 makes a missing one a failure (Windows runs the pure-Go tests only):

  • a KRL written by ssh-keygen -k with every serial encoding, key IDs, three CAs plus “any CA”, explicit keys and a revoked CA key: IsRevoked answers like ssh-keygen -Q for 250 certificates, and Builder given the same revocations writes the same bytes;
  • 40 random serial sets written by both: byte-identical, and the same answers for about 9000 certificates;
  • every truncation and about 1400 single-byte corruptions: Parse refuses exactly what ssh-keygen refuses;
  • the expiry extension loads in ssh-keygen, and the same section marked critical is refused;
  • merged lists revoke exactly what one of their sources revokes.
